content: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, second only to Down syndrome as a cause of mental retardation. This condition arises due to a dynamic mutation in a specific gene located on the long arm of the X chromosome. Various strategies have been developed to screen for this condition during pregnancy. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether screening for fragile X carrier status in women who are considered to be at low risk, either before conception or during pregnancy, provides any additional benefits compared to the current practice of testing only women who are believed to be at higher risk. High-risk women are typically identified based on a family history of fragile X syndrome or other undiagnosed intellectual disabilities or mental illnesses. To investigate this, a search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of October 2008. The study aimed to include randomized clinical trials that compared two groups: one group of women who were tested for fragile X carrier status regardless of their family history (intervention group) and another group of women who were tested only if they had a family history of fragile X syndrome or related conditions (control group). Three independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials. However, no randomized trials meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. As a result, the authors concluded that there is no evidence from randomized trials to determine whether routine screening for fragile X carrier status in low-risk women, either before conception or during pregnancy, offers any advantage over the current practice of testing only women considered to be at increased risk.
